definition: to choose not to do or have something

examples.text: Three delegates abstained from the vote, and the motion failed by one.
Patients were told to abstain from food for twelve hours before the test.
I abstained from dessert because I had already eaten two cookies in the kitchen.

confused.note: Both mean to hold back; abstain often means giving something up as a deliberate choice, or declining to vote.

questions.passage: Because the chairwoman's brother owned one of the companies bidding for the contract, she felt she could not judge the offers fairly. When the board voted, she chose to ______.
questions.explanation: Declining to vote because of a conflict of interest is holding back from taking part.

distractors.why: Coerce means to force someone, and it needs an object; it does not describe staying out of a vote.
Conjecture means to guess, which is not what she did.
Allude means to refer indirectly, which does not complete "she chose to."

definition: to stop someone from doing what they planned, or to stop a plan from succeeding

examples.text: A sudden storm thwarted the fleet's attempt to land at dawn.
The plant's waxy coating thwarts insects that try to lay eggs on its leaves.
Rain thwarted our plan for a rooftop picnic.

confused.note: Thwart means to block a plan; warp means to bend out of shape.

questions.passage: The thieves had studied the gallery's alarm system for months. Their plan was ______ by something they had not foreseen: a night guard who decided, for once, to walk his rounds in the opposite direction.
questions.explanation: An unexpected guard stopped the plan from succeeding.

distractors.why: Facilitated means made easier, the opposite of what the guard did.
Juxtaposed means placed side by side for comparison, which does not fit.
Evinced means showed clearly, which does not describe stopping a plan.

definition: spending money or resources freely and wastefully

examples.text: The prodigal heir ran through his father's fortune in three years.
The parable's prodigal son returns home with empty pockets.
I was prodigal with my data plan and ran out by the tenth of the month.

confused.note: Prodigal means wasteful; a prodigy is a young person with exceptional talent.

questions.passage: Her parents had saved carefully all their lives. She, by contrast, was ______: within a year of receiving her inheritance she had bought two sports cars and a yacht she never learned to sail.
questions.explanation: Buying cars and an unused yacht within a year is wasteful spending.

distractors.why: Frugal means careful with money, which describes her parents.
Servile means overly eager to obey, which is unrelated to spending.
Reluctant means unwilling, but she spent eagerly.

partsNote: from Latin prodigere, "to drive away, to squander"

definition: too eager to obey and please others

examples.text: The servile courtiers praised every word the emperor spoke.
The clerk's servile bowing disgusts the heroine.
There is a difference between being polite to your boss and being servile.

confused.note: Servile means slavishly obedient; civil means polite.

questions.passage: The minister surrounded himself with ______ advisers. None of them ever questioned his decisions; instead they competed to agree with him first and praise him loudest.
questions.explanation: Competing to agree and praise shows excessive eagerness to please.

distractors.why: Defiant means openly resisting, the opposite of these advisers.
Sanguine means optimistic, which is not what the passage describes.
Idiosyncratic means peculiar to an individual, which does not fit.

definition: lazy; wanting to avoid work or effort

examples.text: The indolent heir spends his days on a sofa, ringing for tea.
Reformers blamed indolent officials for the unrepaired roads.
On Sundays I am happily indolent and do not leave the couch before noon.

confused.note: Indolent means lazy; insolent means rude and disrespectful.

questions.passage: The teacher suspected that the student was not incapable but merely ______. When a topic happened to interest him he produced excellent work; otherwise he did the least he could and napped through the rest.
questions.explanation: Doing the minimum and napping shows laziness, not inability.

distractors.why: Diligent means hardworking, the opposite of his usual behavior.
Poignant means deeply moving, which does not describe a student's habits.
Transparent means see-through or open, which is not at issue.

partsNote: from Latin dolere, "to feel pain": taking no pains

definition: causing a strong feeling of sadness or sympathy

examples.text: The novel's most poignant scene shows the old soldier returning to an empty house.
The museum displays a poignant letter from a child evacuated during the war.
Finding my grandfather's handwriting in an old cookbook was unexpectedly poignant.

confused.note: Poignant means emotionally touching; pungent means sharply strong in smell or taste.

questions.passage: The photograph is especially ______ because of what the viewer knows and its subjects do not. The young couple are laughing on the pier, unaware that the storm visible on the horizon will destroy their town by morning.
questions.explanation: Knowing what awaits the happy couple makes the image deeply moving.

distractors.why: Serene means peaceful; the viewer's knowledge makes the image sad, not calm.
Momentous means of great importance, which does not capture the sadness.
Tangential means only slightly related, which does not fit.

definition: calm and peaceful

examples.text: The story ends with a serene evening on the lake, all quarrels forgotten.
Seen from orbit, the hurricane looks strangely serene.
The baby looked serene in her sleep after an hour of crying.

confused.note: Serene is the adjective; serenity is the noun.

questions.passage: Travelers arriving from the crowded capital are struck by how ______ the island is. There are no cars, the only regular sounds are waves and goat bells, and the single shop closes for three hours every afternoon.
questions.explanation: No cars, soft sounds, and long quiet afternoons describe a peaceful place.

distractors.why: Volatile means unstable and explosive, the opposite of this island.
Intricate means complicated, which a quiet island is not.
Momentous means historically important, which is not the quality described.

definition: to force someone to do something by using threats or pressure

examples.text: The regime coerced farmers into selling their grain below cost.
The villain coerces the clerk into forging the will.
You cannot coerce a toddler into eating peas; you can only negotiate.

confused.note: To coerce is to force with threats; to coax is to persuade gently.

questions.passage: The confession was thrown out by the court. Judges found that the police had ______ the suspect, questioning him for thirty hours without sleep and threatening to arrest his family if he refused to sign.
questions.explanation: Sleep deprivation and threats are force, not free choice.

distractors.why: Coaxed means gently persuaded, far too mild for threats and thirty hours without sleep.
Thwarted means blocked a plan, which does not describe forcing a confession.
Invoked means called upon a law or authority, which does not fit.

definition: cheerfully hopeful and confident about the future

examples.text: The general remained sanguine even as his supply lines grew longer.
Researchers are sanguine about the vaccine's chances in the next trial.
I am not sanguine about finishing this essay by midnight.

confused.note: Sanguine means optimistic; sanguinary means bloody.

questions.passage: Analysts warned that the new shop faced too much competition to survive. Its owner was more ______, pointing to steady growth in sales and predicting that she would open a second location within a year.
questions.explanation: Predicting expansion despite warnings shows cheerful confidence.

distractors.why: Despondent means hopeless, the opposite of her outlook.
Callous means unfeeling, which is not what the passage describes.
Servile means slavishly obedient, which does not fit.

definition: impossible to stop or change

examples.text: The inexorable advance of the glacier carved the valley over thousands of years.
The army's inexorable march reached the capital in a month.
The inexorable approach of Monday morning ruined my Sunday night.

confused.note: Inexorable means unstoppable; inexplicable means impossible to explain.

questions.passage: Villagers tried sandbags, stone walls, and finally a concrete barrier. None of it mattered: the sea's ______ rise continued year after year, and the lowest row of houses was eventually abandoned.
questions.explanation: A rise that no barrier could halt is impossible to stop.

distractors.why: Sporadic means occasional, but the rise continued every year.
Hypothetical means imagined or supposed, but this rise was real.
Tangential means only slightly related, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin orare, "to plead": not to be moved by pleading

definition: to reach a conclusion from evidence and reasoning

examples.text: From the tooth's shape, scientists inferred that the animal ate plants.
Readers must infer the narrator's age from small clues in the first chapter.
I inferred from the empty driveway that nobody was home.

confused.note: A speaker or a piece of evidence implies; a listener or reader infers.

questions.passage: No written record explains why the settlement was abandoned. Archaeologists ______ from the layer of ash covering its houses that the inhabitants fled a volcanic eruption.
questions.explanation: The archaeologists reason from evidence to a conclusion.

distractors.why: Imply means to suggest; evidence implies, but people who reason from it infer.
Abstain means to hold back from doing something, which is not what they do.
Juxtapose means to place side by side, which does not fit reasoning from ash.

definition: unusual in a way that is particular to one person or thing

examples.text: The poet's idiosyncratic punctuation, all dashes and no commas, is instantly recognizable.
The duke kept an idiosyncratic calendar of his own invention.
My dad has an idiosyncratic filing system that only he can navigate.

confused.note: Idiosyncratic means distinctively individual; it has nothing to do with being foolish.

questions.passage: The cartographer's maps are easy to identify because of their ______ style. Where other mapmakers drew mountains as simple triangles, he sketched each peak as a tiny sleeping animal.
questions.explanation: A style no other mapmaker shared is peculiar to one person.

distractors.why: Orthodox means conventional, the opposite of his unique style.
Dormant means inactive, which does not describe a drawing style.
Inexorable means unstoppable, which does not fit.

definition: able to be seen through; or open and honest, with nothing hidden

examples.text: The jellyfish is almost completely transparent in clear water.
The new council promised a transparent budget that any citizen could read.
His excuse was so transparent that even he started laughing.

confused.note: Transparent lets you see clearly through; translucent lets light through but blurs what is behind.

questions.passage: To rebuild public trust, the agency pledged to be more ______. It now posts every contract online, publishes the minutes of its meetings, and allows reporters to attend budget hearings.
questions.explanation: Posting contracts and opening meetings means hiding nothing.

distractors.why: Covert means secret, the opposite of the agency's pledge.
Prodigal means wasteful, which the agency would not pledge to be.
Indolent means lazy, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin parere, "to appear": showing through

definition: unwilling and hesitant to do something

examples.text: The reluctant king signed the charter only when the barons surrounded his tent.
A reluctant hero, he would have preferred to stay home with his books.
I was reluctant to try sushi, but now I ask for it every birthday.

confused.note: Reluctant means unwilling to do something; reticent means unwilling to speak.

questions.passage: The author had always avoided publicity. She was therefore ______ to appear on television, agreeing only after her publisher pointed out that the interview would help fund the village library she cared about.
questions.explanation: Agreeing only after persuasion shows she was unwilling at first.

distractors.why: Zealous means intensely enthusiastic, the opposite of someone who avoids publicity.
Sanguine means optimistic, which is not her attitude toward appearing.
Inexorable means unstoppable, which does not describe a hesitant person.

partsNote: from Latin luctari, "to struggle": struggling against

definition: not active or growing now, but able to become active later

examples.text: The volcano has been dormant for three centuries but is not extinct.
The old rivalry lay dormant until the border was redrawn.
My gym membership has been dormant since February.

confused.note: A dormant volcano may erupt again; an extinct one will not.

questions.passage: Many bulbs survive the winter in a ______ state. Buried in frozen soil, they show no growth for months, then send up shoots within days of the first warm rain.
questions.explanation: Showing no growth but able to sprout later is being inactive for a time.

distractors.why: Volatile means unstable and quick to change, which a buried bulb is not.
Poignant means emotionally moving, which does not describe a bulb.
Servile means overly obedient, which does not fit.

definition: an opinion or conclusion based on incomplete information; a guess

examples.text: Until the probe arrives, the moon's ocean remains a matter of conjecture.
How the builders raised the stones is still conjecture.
Who ate the last slice is pure conjecture, though I have suspicions.

confused.note: A conjecture is a guess; a conjuncture is a combination of events.

questions.passage: The biographer admits that her account of the painter's childhood is largely ______. No letters or school records survive, and she has had to piece the story together from a few remarks the painter made late in life.
questions.explanation: An account pieced together without records is educated guesswork.

distractors.why: Dogma is belief held as unquestionably true, the opposite of an admitted guess.
Efficacy means effectiveness, which does not describe an account.
A dearth is a shortage; it cannot describe what the account is.

definition: to show a feeling or quality clearly

examples.text: The letters evince a tenderness that the stern general never showed in public.
The crowd evinced little enthusiasm for the new tax.
My dog evinces deep suspicion whenever the vacuum cleaner comes out.

confused.note: To evince is to show a feeling you have; to evoke is to call up a feeling in someone else.

questions.passage: Though she said little during the tour of the laboratory, the visiting scientist ______ great interest in the work, leaning in to study each instrument and photographing several pages of the team's notes.
questions.explanation: Her actions clearly showed interest.

distractors.why: Feigned means pretended; nothing suggests her interest was fake.
Thwarted means blocked, which does not fit showing a feeling.
Eschewed means deliberately avoided, the opposite of leaning in to look.

partsNote: from Latin vincere, "to conquer, to prove"

definition: new and different from anything known before

examples.text: The lab found a novel way to store hydrogen at room temperature.
Paying workers enough to buy the cars they built was a novel idea in 1914.
Dipping fries in a milkshake was a novel experience, and a good one.

confused.note: Novel means new; a novice is a beginner.

questions.passage: Earlier engineers had tried to strengthen the bridge by adding more steel. Tanaka's approach was ______: she proposed removing weight instead, replacing the heavy concrete deck with a lighter one that the existing cables could easily support.
questions.explanation: Doing the reverse of what earlier engineers tried is a new approach.

distractors.why: Orthodox means following accepted practice, the opposite of her idea.
Tangential means only loosely related, but her idea addressed the problem directly.
Dormant means inactive, which does not describe an approach.

definition: to act against something to reduce its effect

examples.text: The drug counteracts the venom by blocking it from reaching nerve cells.
The city planted trees to counteract the smoke from its mills.
I drink water with spicy food, though milk counteracts the heat better.

confused.note: Counteract means to work against; counterfeit means fake.

questions.passage: High altitude thins the blood's supply of oxygen. To ______ this effect, the body gradually produces more red blood cells, which is why climbers spend days at base camp before attempting a summit.
questions.explanation: Producing more red cells works against the lack of oxygen.

distractors.why: Amplify means to increase, but the body is offsetting the effect.
Evince means to show clearly, which is not what the extra cells do.
Infer means to conclude from evidence, which does not fit.

definition: very important because of its effects on the future

examples.text: The signing of the charter was a momentous event in the nation's story.
The first image of a black hole was a momentous achievement.
Choosing a college felt like the most momentous decision of my life so far.

confused.note: Momentous means very important; momentary means lasting only a moment.

questions.passage: At the time, the meeting seemed routine, and newspapers gave it a single paragraph. Only later did its ______ nature become clear: the agreement reached that afternoon would shape trade across the continent for fifty years.
questions.explanation: An agreement shaping fifty years of trade is highly important.

distractors.why: Trivial means unimportant, which is how the meeting wrongly seemed.
Momentary means brief; it resembles the right word but means something else.
Serene means calm, which is not the point of the contrast.

partsNote: from "moment" in the sense of importance

definition: only slightly connected to the main subject

examples.text: The essay wanders into tangential stories about the author's cats.
The reviewer asked the authors to cut a tangential section on bird migration.
The meeting ran long because of tangential debates about lunch.

confused.note: Tangential means barely related; tangible means able to be touched or clearly real.

questions.passage: The lecture was supposed to concern the causes of the 1929 crash. The speaker spent most of the hour on ______ matters, including his grandfather's career as a banker and the architecture of the stock exchange building.
questions.explanation: Family stories and architecture are only loosely tied to the announced topic.

distractors.why: Pertinent means directly relevant, the opposite of these digressions.
Momentous means highly important, which these side topics were not.
Intricate means complicated; the problem is that the material was off topic.

definition: to place two things side by side, especially to compare or contrast them

examples.text: The novel juxtaposes scenes of a royal banquet with scenes of a village famine.
The exhibit juxtaposes soldiers' letters with the official reports of the same battles.
The yearbook juxtaposes our first-grade photos with our senior portraits.

confused.note: To juxtapose is to set side by side; to superimpose is to lay one on top of another.

questions.passage: The photographer likes to ______ the old and the new. In her best known image, a horse-drawn cart waits at a traffic light beside a row of electric cars.
questions.explanation: Placing a cart beside electric cars sets two things side by side for contrast.

distractors.why: Conflate means to merge two things as if they were one; she sets them apart for contrast.
Thwart means to block, which is not what the image does.
Abstain means to hold back, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin juxta, "next to": to place next to

definition: likely to change suddenly and unpredictably, especially for the worse

examples.text: Gasoline is volatile and evaporates quickly at room temperature.
The border region remained volatile for years after the war ended.
The price of concert tickets is so volatile that I check it every hour.

confused.note: Volatile means unstable; versatile means able to do many things.

questions.passage: Investors seeking steady returns are advised to avoid the currency. Its value is extremely ______: in a single week last spring it rose by a third, fell by half, and then recovered most of its losses.
questions.explanation: Huge swings within a week show sudden, unpredictable change.

distractors.why: Dormant means inactive, the opposite of wild swings.
Transparent means open or see-through, which does not describe price swings.
Reluctant means unwilling, which a currency cannot be.

definition: having many small parts or details arranged in a complicated way

examples.text: The intricate network of veins in a leaf carries water to every cell.
Court life was governed by an intricate code of bows and titles.
She folded the paper into an intricate crane in under a minute.

confused.note: Intricate means complicated in detail; integral means essential to the whole.

questions.passage: Under a magnifying glass the watch's mechanism is astonishingly ______. More than three hundred gears, springs, and levers, some thinner than a hair, fit together inside a case the size of a coin.
questions.explanation: Hundreds of tiny interlocking parts make a complicated, detailed mechanism.

distractors.why: Rudimentary means basic and undeveloped, the opposite of this mechanism.
Volatile means unstable, which a precise watch is not.
Poignant means emotionally moving, which does not describe gears.

definition: to mention something indirectly, without naming it outright

examples.text: The poem alludes to the fall of Troy without ever naming the city.
In his speech the king alluded to "recent troubles" but never said the word "revolt."
Mom alluded to a surprise this weekend and then refused to say more.

confused.note: Allude means to refer indirectly; elude means to escape or avoid.

questions.passage: The senator never mentioned her rival by name. She did, however, ______ to him several times, remarking that "some people in this chamber" seemed to prefer television cameras to committee work.
questions.explanation: Speaking of "some people" without a name is referring to him indirectly.

distractors.why: Elude means to escape; it sounds like the right word but does not mean to refer.
Abstain means to refrain, which does not fit "to him several times."
Coerce means to force, which is not what her remarks do.

definition: to deliberately avoid or keep away from something

examples.text: The novelist eschews adjectives and lets the verbs do the work.
The sect eschewed all ornament, even buttons on their coats.
My grandmother eschews microwaves and reheats everything on the stove.

confused.note: Eschew (es-CHOO) means to avoid on principle; it has nothing to do with chewing.

questions.passage: While her competitors rely on expensive advertising, the bakery's owner ______ it entirely. She spends nothing on promotion, trusting that customers who taste her bread will tell their friends.
questions.explanation: Spending nothing on promotion is deliberately avoiding advertising.

distractors.why: Espouses means supports or adopts, the opposite of avoiding.
Invokes means calls upon, which does not fit avoiding advertising.
Induces means brings about or persuades, which is not what she does to advertising.

definition: mysterious and difficult to understand

examples.text: The enigmatic stranger answers every question with another question.
The enigmatic symbols on the stone have never been deciphered.
She gave an enigmatic smile when I asked what my birthday gift was.

confused.note: Enigmatic means puzzling; dogmatic means rigidly opinionated.

questions.passage: The sculptor rarely explained her work, and her titles offered no help. One piece, a bronze door standing alone in a field, is simply called "Tuesday," an ______ label that visitors have debated for decades.
questions.explanation: A title that explains nothing and provokes decades of debate is puzzling.

distractors.why: Explicit means clearly stated, the opposite of this mysterious title.
Pertinent means relevant; the title's link to the work is exactly what is unclear.
Lucrative means profitable, which does not describe a title.

definition: following generally accepted beliefs, rules, or practices

examples.text: Her theory challenged the orthodox view that the disease was inherited.
The orthodox clergy opposed any change to the old rites.
His chess openings are orthodox, but his endgames are full of surprises.

confused.note: Orthodox means holding accepted beliefs; heterodox means departing from them.

questions.passage: Most economists of the time held the ______ position that governments should cut spending during a slump. Keynes broke with his colleagues, arguing that this was precisely when governments ought to spend more.
questions.explanation: A position most economists held is the accepted, conventional one.

distractors.why: Radical means departing sharply from the accepted view, which describes Keynes.
Callous means unfeeling, which is not the point of the contrast.
Sporadic means occasional, which does not describe a position.

partsNote: from Greek orthos, "straight, correct": correct belief

definition: the ability to produce the result that is wanted

examples.text: The trial tested the efficacy of the drug against three strains of the virus.
Doctors of the 1700s argued over the efficacy of bleeding patients.
I doubt the efficacy of studying with the television on.

confused.note: Efficacy is whether something works; efficiency is how little time or energy it wastes.

questions.passage: Before the new fertilizer could be sold, regulators required proof of its ______. The manufacturer therefore planted two hundred test fields, treating half of them, and compared the harvests.
questions.explanation: Comparing harvests tests whether the fertilizer actually works.

distractors.why: Paucity means scarcity, which regulators would not ask to be proved.
A dearth is a shortage, which does not fit.
Conjecture is guesswork, the opposite of proof from field tests.

definition: based on an imagined situation, not a real one

examples.text: The paper describes a hypothetical planet with twice Earth's gravity.
Historians enjoy the hypothetical question of what would have happened had the fleet arrived on time.
"What would you do with a million dollars?" is a fun hypothetical question.

confused.note: Hypothetical means imagined for the sake of argument; hypocritical means saying one thing and doing another.

questions.passage: The ethics professor does not ask students about real court cases. She prefers ______ ones, inventing situations, such as a lifeboat with one seat too few, in which every choice has a cost.
questions.explanation: Invented situations are imagined, not real.

distractors.why: Empirical means based on real observation, the opposite of invented cases.
Inconsequential means unimportant; her cases are imaginary but serious.
Contrite means remorseful, which does not describe a case.

definition: suggested or understood without being stated directly

examples.text: There is an implicit warning in the old woman's story.
The treaty carried an implicit promise of protection.
When I borrowed the car, the implicit agreement was that I would refill the tank.

confused.note: Implicit means suggested without being said; explicit means stated outright.

questions.passage: Nothing in the job posting says that applicants must live nearby. That requirement is ______, however, in the statement that employees are expected at the office by six each morning.
questions.explanation: The requirement is not stated but can be understood from the early start time.

distractors.why: Explicit means stated directly, which the first sentence rules out.
Adverse means harmful or unfavorable, which does not fit.
Sporadic means occasional, which does not describe a requirement.

definition: to make it difficult for someone to do something or for something to happen

examples.text: Thick fog hindered the search for the missing boat.
Poor roads hindered the delivery of grain to the capital.
My broken glasses hindered my attempt to read the menu.

confused.note: Hinder is the verb; hindrance is the noun.

questions.passage: The expedition's progress was ______ at every turn. Deep snow slowed the sleds, two of the dogs fell ill, and a broken compass forced the team to wait for clear nights to navigate by the stars.
questions.explanation: Snow, sick dogs, and a broken compass made progress difficult.

distractors.why: Expedited means sped up, the opposite of these delays.
Ascertained means found out for certain, which does not fit progress.
Denounced means publicly condemned, which snow and illness cannot do.

definition: directly related to the subject being considered

examples.text: Please include only data pertinent to the question of water quality.
The lawyer produced a pertinent letter written a week before the fire.
Her question about cost was pertinent, since we had only twenty dollars.

confused.note: Pertinent means relevant; impertinent usually means rude, not irrelevant.

questions.passage: The judge reminded the witness to confine her testimony to ______ matters. What she had eaten for breakfast and her opinion of the defendant's taste in music, he said, had no bearing on the case.
questions.explanation: Matters with a bearing on the case are relevant ones.

distractors.why: Peripheral means of minor relevance, which describes what the judge wants excluded.
Hypothetical means imagined, which is not the distinction the judge draws.
Potent means powerful, which does not fit.

definition: to call on a law, rule, authority, or idea as a reason or for support

examples.text: The governor invoked emergency powers to close the port.
The poet invokes the muse in the opening line.
My sister invoked the "I called it first" rule to claim the front seat.

confused.note: To invoke is to call on a rule or authority; to evoke is to bring a feeling or memory to mind.

questions.passage: Rather than answer the committee's questions, the executive chose to ______ her legal right to remain silent, a protection that witnesses may claim when their answers might be used against them.
questions.explanation: Claiming a legal protection is calling on a right.

distractors.why: Evoke means to bring a feeling to mind; it is a look-alike that does not fit a legal right.
Eschew means to avoid, but she is using the right, not avoiding it.
Hinder means to obstruct, which is not what one does to one's own right.

definition: to find out something for certain

examples.text: The first step was to ascertain whether the samples had been contaminated.
Investigators never ascertained who had set the fire.
I called the restaurant to ascertain whether it was open on Mondays.

confused.note: Ascertain means to find out for sure; assert means to state firmly.

questions.passage: Before repairing the mural, conservators needed to ______ what kind of paint the artist had used. They sent a tiny flake to a laboratory, which identified it as an oil mixed with beeswax.
questions.explanation: Sending a sample to a lab is a way of finding out for certain.

distractors.why: Assert means to state firmly; conservators needed to learn the fact, not declare it.
Induce means to bring about, which does not fit learning a fact.
Denounce means to condemn publicly, which is unrelated.

definition: happening only sometimes, at irregular intervals

examples.text: The region gets only sporadic rain, sometimes none for a year.
Sporadic fighting continued along the border long after the truce.
My attempts at keeping a journal have been sporadic at best.

confused.note: Both mean irregular; sporadic stresses scattered occurrence, spasmodic stresses sudden bursts.

questions.passage: Bus service to the village is ______. A bus may come twice in one morning and then not again for three days, so most residents no longer bother to wait at the stop.
questions.explanation: Buses arriving at unpredictable, scattered times are irregular and occasional.

distractors.why: Incessant means nonstop, the opposite of buses that rarely come.
Lucrative means profitable, which is not what the passage describes.
Orthodox means conventional, which does not fit.

definition: to say publicly that someone or something is wrong or evil

examples.text: The pamphlet denounced the tax as theft.
In the final act the daughter denounces her father before the whole court.
The coach denounced the rumor that she was leaving for a rival school.

confused.note: To denounce is to condemn publicly; to renounce is to give something up.

questions.passage: The newspaper's editorial did not merely question the new policy. It ______ the plan in the strongest terms, calling it "a betrayal of every promise this government has made."
questions.explanation: Calling the plan a betrayal is strong public condemnation.

distractors.why: Endorsed means publicly supported, the opposite of this editorial.
Renounced means gave up a claim or belief; the newspaper condemned the plan, it did not give anything up.
Ascertained means found out for certain, which does not fit.

definition: not caring about other people's feelings or suffering

examples.text: The landlord's callous reply to the widow's plea turns the whole village against him.
The general's callous disregard for his own soldiers shocked the reporters.
Laughing at someone who trips is callous, even if the fall looked funny.

confused.note: Callous is the adjective meaning unfeeling; a callus is a patch of hardened skin.

questions.passage: Readers were outraged by the company's ______ response to the flood. While families waited on rooftops, its only public statement concerned the effect of the disaster on quarterly profits.
questions.explanation: Discussing profits while families are stranded shows no care for suffering.

distractors.why: Contrite means remorseful, which the company was not.
Compassionate means caring, the opposite of this response.
Enigmatic means mysterious; the response was clear and cold.

definition: a lack or shortage of something

examples.text: A dearth of data from the deep ocean limits what models can predict.
The dearth of timber forced shipbuilders to import oak from abroad.
There is a dearth of good snacks in this house.

confused.note: Dearth (rhymes with "earth") means shortage; it is not related to death.

questions.passage: The clinic's problem is not a lack of patients or equipment. It is a ______ of trained nurses: twelve positions have been open for more than a year, and only two applicants have come forward.
questions.explanation: Many open positions and few applicants show a shortage.

distractors.why: A surplus is more than enough, the opposite of unfilled positions.
Efficacy means effectiveness, which does not fit "of trained nurses."
A precedent is an earlier example, which does not fit.

definition: not important; having little effect

examples.text: The difference between the two readings was inconsequential.
The lovers quarrel over an inconsequential remark about a hat.
Whether we leave at 8:00 or 8:05 is inconsequential.

confused.note: Inconsequential means unimportant; inconsistent means not staying the same.

questions.passage: The editor assured the author that the changes were ______. A comma had been moved on page forty and a date corrected on page ninety, and nothing else in the book had been touched.
questions.explanation: A moved comma and one corrected date are small, unimportant changes.

distractors.why: Momentous means highly important, the opposite of these tiny edits.
Adverse means harmful, which small corrections are not.
Implicit means unstated, which does not describe the changes.

definition: useful or convenient for a purpose, though not always right or fair

examples.text: The king found it expedient to marry his rival's daughter.
The lawyer chooses the expedient lie over the awkward truth.
Taking the shortcut across the lawn was expedient, if not polite.

confused.note: Expedient is an adjective meaning convenient; expedite is a verb meaning to speed up.

questions.passage: The mayor admitted that closing the shelter was not the most humane choice. It was merely the most ______ one, since it balanced the budget quickly and required no vote by the council.
questions.explanation: A choice that is quick and convenient but not the most humane is expedient.

distractors.why: Compassionate means caring, which the mayor admits the choice was not.
Arduous means very difficult, but this option was the easy one.
Hypothetical means imagined, but the closing was real.

partsNote: from Latin pes, "foot": freeing the feet

definition: a very small amount of something; less than is needed

examples.text: The paucity of fossils from that period makes dating difficult.
A paucity of written records leaves the kingdom's early years obscure.
The paucity of outlets in the library sends students hunting for a seat by the wall.

confused.note: Paucity means scarcity of anything; poverty means lack of money in particular.

questions.passage: Historians of the ancient city work under a serious handicap. Because of the ______ of surviving documents, fewer than thirty in all, most of what they claim about its government is educated guesswork.
questions.explanation: Fewer than thirty documents is a very small supply.

distractors.why: A plethora is an excess, the opposite of so few documents.
Efficacy means effectiveness, which does not fit.
Veracity means truthfulness; the handicap described is how few documents survive.

definition: feeling sorry and guilty for something you did wrong

examples.text: The contrite thief returns the necklace with a letter of apology.
The contrite minister resigned and repaid the missing funds.
My dog looked so contrite beside the chewed shoe that I could not stay angry.

confused.note: Contrite means remorseful; contrived means artificial and forced.

questions.passage: The driver who had scraped the parked car did not flee. She left a note with her phone number, and when the owner called she was ______, apologizing three times and offering to pay for the repair that same day.
questions.explanation: Repeated apology and an offer to pay show sincere remorse.

distractors.why: Callous means unfeeling, the opposite of her response.
Loquacious means talkative; the point is her remorse, not how much she spoke.
Expedient means convenient, which does not describe her attitude.

partsNote: from Latin terere, "to rub, to wear down": worn down by guilt

definition: talking a great deal

examples.text: The loquacious barber narrates the town's entire history during a single haircut.
The loquacious senator once spoke for fourteen hours without sitting down.
My loquacious lab partner makes every five-minute task take twenty.

confused.note: Loquacious means speaking a lot; eloquent means speaking well.

questions.passage: Interviewers love the retired pilot because she is so ______. A single question about her first flight can produce forty minutes of stories, each leading without pause into the next.
questions.explanation: Forty minutes of stories from one question shows she talks a great deal.

distractors.why: Taciturn means saying little, the opposite of this pilot.
Contrite means remorseful, which is unrelated.
Callous means unfeeling, which does not fit.

definition: stated clearly and in detail, leaving no room for doubt

examples.text: The protocol gives explicit instructions for every step of the procedure.
The charter made an explicit promise of free trade.
My parents were explicit: home by eleven, no exceptions.

confused.note: Explicit means stated outright; implicit means suggested without being said.

questions.passage: Earlier contracts had merely implied that the builder would repair any defects. The new one is ______ on the point, stating in its first paragraph that all repairs for ten years will be made at the builder's expense.
questions.explanation: A clear statement in the first paragraph leaves no doubt.

distractors.why: Implicit means unstated, which describes the earlier contracts.
Enigmatic means puzzling, the opposite of a clear statement.
Inconsequential means unimportant, which a ten-year guarantee is not.

definition: harmful or unfavorable

examples.text: The drug was withdrawn after reports of adverse effects on the liver.
Adverse winds kept the fleet in harbor for a month.
Despite adverse weather, the game went ahead.

confused.note: Adverse describes conditions or effects that are harmful; averse describes a person who is opposed to something.

questions.passage: The marathon was run in ______ conditions. A cold rain fell throughout, a headwind slowed the runners on the long final stretch, and several sections of the course were under water.
questions.explanation: Rain, headwind, and flooding are unfavorable conditions.

distractors.why: Averse describes a person who dislikes something; conditions are adverse.
Lucrative means profitable, which does not describe weather.
Pertinent means relevant, which does not fit.

definition: very strong, powerful, or effective

examples.text: The venom is so potent that a single drop can stop a heart.
The cartoon became a potent symbol of resistance.
This hot sauce is potent, so start with one drop.

confused.note: Potent means powerful; a portent is a sign of something to come.

questions.passage: Chemists warn that the cleaning agent is far more ______ than ordinary household products. A spoonful diluted in a bucket of water is enough to strip paint, and it should never be used without gloves.
questions.explanation: A spoonful that strips paint is very strong.

distractors.why: Innocuous means harmless, the opposite of a paint-stripping chemical.
Sporadic means occasional, which does not describe strength.
Implicit means unstated, which does not fit.

definition: at the edge of something; of minor importance

examples.text: Peripheral vision lets you notice movement at the side while looking straight ahead.
The island played only a peripheral role in the war.
Decorations are peripheral; the party needs food and music first.

confused.note: Peripheral means at the edge or secondary; perpetual means never ending.

questions.passage: The report devotes thirty pages to questions that are ______ at best, such as the color of the new buses and the design of the tickets. The central issue, how the system will be paid for, receives a single paragraph.
questions.explanation: Bus colors and ticket design are side matters compared with funding.

distractors.why: Pertinent means directly relevant, which is how the neglected central issue would be described.
Potent means powerful, which does not describe minor questions.
Explicit means clearly stated, which is not the contrast with "central."

definition: to cause something to happen, or to persuade someone to do something

examples.text: The drug induces sleep within twenty minutes.
Free land induced thousands of families to move west.
Nothing could induce my brother to eat mushrooms.

confused.note: Induce means to cause or persuade; deduce means to reach a conclusion by reasoning.

questions.passage: The city has tried several schemes to ______ commuters to leave their cars at home, including cheaper train fares, new bicycle lanes, and a toll on drivers who enter the center at rush hour.
questions.explanation: Fares, lanes, and tolls are meant to persuade commuters to change their behavior.

distractors.why: Deduce means to reason to a conclusion; it resembles the right word but does not mean persuade.
Denounce means to condemn, and it does not fit "commuters to leave."
Hinder means to obstruct, but the city wants to encourage this choice.

definition: producing a lot of money; profitable

examples.text: The spice trade was so lucrative that nations went to war over it.
Patents on the new process proved lucrative for the university.
Babysitting on New Year's Eve is surprisingly lucrative.

confused.note: Lucrative means profitable; ludicrous means ridiculous.

questions.passage: Few people expected a business that rents out goats to clear weeds to succeed. It has proved remarkably ______, however: its owners earned back their investment in eight months and now turn customers away.
questions.explanation: Recovering the investment quickly and turning customers away shows it is profitable.

distractors.why: Callous means unfeeling, which does not describe a business's success.
Peripheral means of minor importance, which contradicts its success.
Adverse means unfavorable, the opposite of how the business turned out.
